extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; general literate public and potential contributors (early 18th-century polite society)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and prescriptive social advice found in The Spectator: what kinds of submissions will be accepted, stylistic and topical expectations for contributors, and norms of polite conversation and public behaviour. Also includes recommendations for public-minded reportage (charity, trades, inventions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributors should send Discourses with their Names and Places of Abode so the editor can be satisfied the writings are authentick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only pieces accompanied by author identification and place will be inserted; this is required so the editor can verify authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad subject scope (include mechanical arts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper should not confine itself to learning and morality; mechanick arts, ways of gain, husbandry, and thrift should have their place as well as the liberal arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical topics useful to a greater number of people (trades, industry practices, how people gained success) are explicitly invited alongside literary or philosophical pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical usefulness / profitable information
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributions that give profitable information to the public—practical rules, histories of trade success, or instructive accounts—are especially valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: histories of shops, accounts of land purchases, histories of stocks and their rises/falls, treatises from 'Change-Alley'—material that helps readers in real pursuits (wealth, trade, thrift).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of minor inventions and artificers
rubrics_metrics.description: Both grand inventions and small practical improvements by artificers merit notice and recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor invites writings from inventors 'from the late noble Inventor of the Longitude ... to the humble Author of Strops for Razors'—arguing that small useful arts deserve reception and praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid technical terms; use accessible language
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributors are cautioned against using 'terms of art' or describing familiar things in words unknown to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When soliciting correspondence, the editor warns that such technical language will make the account unintelligible to general readers; writers should explain or omit jargon to ensure broad comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include domestic/domestick instruction and cautionary tales
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestic economy, household virtues, and instructive tragic examples (e.g., cases of bankruptcy) are appropriate topics to awaken caution and guide conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor suggests occasional 'touches of Tragedy' like bankruptcy narratives to show how quickly plenty can turn to penury, thereby instructing readers on prudence and industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not monopolize conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an impertinent and unreasonable fault for one person to take up all the discourse in company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speakers should give others opportunity; periodical writers should not presume to occupy all public discourse to the exclusion of qualified contributors—hence the call for wider contributor participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question and examine scandalous reports before accepting
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not receive impressions to the disadvantage of others without examination; scandal spreads readily and should be checked for source and credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing Cicero: reports without known origin or reliable testimony are too slight to discredit a person's innocence and honour; trace ill reports and reject those arising from frivolous sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not revel in speaking ill of others (avoid malicious gossip)
rubrics_metrics.description: The temper which cannot be pleased except by lamentation or the discredit of others is low and contemptible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scandal-bearing and delight in others' misfortunes are condemned; social actors should resist the appetite for defamation and envy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for withdrawing from company ('Infirmary' model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who recognize certain personal faults (vanity, excessive argumentation, loudness, rustick mirth, habitual complaint, valetudinarian habits) should withdraw from company until reformed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mock 'Infirmary' is proposed where those conscious of such defects retire to reform: e.g., the vain who seek too much applause, the argumentative who cannot consent, the loud talker, habitual complainers, those with crude mirth—self-exclusion preserves polite society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation and decorum in public rooms
rubrics_metrics.description: No one is to appear in public rooms undressed, nor enter abruptly into another's apartment without intimation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe outward propriety: dress appropriately in public spaces and give notice before entering private rooms; breaches may be subject to social sanction (e.g., temporary exclusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Behaviour in gaming: bear ill fortune with good grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Gamers should not show disorderly behaviour when losing (swearing, stamping, throwing down cards); they should practice moderation in victory and loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In petitions for reinstatement after misbehaviour at whist, the offender promises to 'bear ill Fortune with a good Grace' and restrain gestures of passion; gaming etiquette is part of polite conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful charity: attend to genuine poverty and guard against impostors
rubrics_metrics.description: Charity should not be sacrificed to popularity; citizens should pay attention to true objects of charity and work to distinguish impostors from the truly needy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend that an officer (beadle or magistrate) hear the claims of constant beggars and keep order; observe patterns (times, tones) and provide mechanisms for relief while discouraging imposture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unseasonable familiarities in mixed company (married couples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain intimate freedoms or overt fondness by married people in company are indecent and should be corrected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining modesty and restraint in mixed assemblies preserves the comfort of bashful or younger attendees; public correction is advised when such indecencies occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppose petty local and national prejudices; cultivate generous impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not vilify entire bodies (nations, colleges, parishes) out of party spirit or local pride; teach youth to admire excellence wherever it appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer urges removing prejudices from youth by exposing them to admirable persons from less-known societies rather than inflating pride in one's own group; avoid absurd general charges and narrow imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discourage slavish imitation and affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Copying admired men blindly leads to affectation; transcribers often adopt oddities that suit the original but appear ungraceful in imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage originality and showcase diverse examples of excellence so that young minds expand rather than contract into derivative, awkward mimicry.
